lesson.title: Pronoun Gym
lesson.subtitle: mijn, jouw, zijn, haar, ons — possessives agree with the thing owned

hook.title: The Owner Does Not Decide
hook.content: Dutch possessives agree with the thing owned, not with the owner: mijn boek, jouw fiets, zijn huis, haar auto. The owner's gender is irrelevant.

pattern.title: Possessive + noun
pattern.content: Mijn, jouw, zijn, haar, ons and jullie sit before the noun. Onze replaces ons before de-words and plurals: ons huis but onze auto. The form follows the noun.
pattern.trap_note: Do not choose haar because the owner is female; haar agrees with the owned noun's grammatical class, not the owner's sex.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (Pronoun Gym):
exercises.target_answer: mijn, jouw, zijn, haar, ons, jullie
exercises.meaning: my, your (informal), his, her (possessive), our, you (plural)
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "Pronoun Gym": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “My book is here.”?
exercises.explanation: “Mijn boek is hier.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “Pronoun Gym”.

cues: It means: Your book is there.
exercises.explanation: “Jouw boek is daar.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Possessive + noun.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Do not choose haar because the owner is female; haar agrees with the owned noun's grammatical class, not the owner's sex.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Zijn fiets is nieuw.” is word-for-word “His bike is new.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Possessive + noun.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: Her house is big.
exercises.explanation: “Haar huis is groot.” reuses only material taught in “Pronoun Gym” — Possessive + noun.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Haar huis is groot.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Possessive + noun.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “Our house is small.”
twist.explanation: Ons is used before a het-word; onze would be used before a de-word.

summary.outcome: Use the possessive set and choose ons/onze by the noun.
summary.takeaway: Possessives track the owned noun, not the owner.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: Reflexives & Daily Routine.

mijn.etymology_derivation: English mine/my and Dutch mijn are the same possessive.

jouw.etymology_derivation: The possessive that belongs to jij.

zijn_poss.etymology_derivation: The possessive zijn is homographic with the being-verb zijn.

haar_poss.etymology_derivation: The possessive haar is homographic with haar ('hair').

ons_poss.etymology_derivation: The possessive ons; onze is used before de-words and plurals.

jullie.etymology_derivation: Historically jij plus lui ('people'): a transparent plural you, unlike English.
